title: Athens and Thessaloniki: North vs South

blocks.title: Πάνω και κάτω: two cities, one language
blocks.text:
Greek has a standard language based mostly on southern (Peloponnesian and old Athenian-area) speech, and Athens, with roughly a third of the population, sets the tone of television, advertising and the internet. Thessaloniki, the second city, is officially called **η συμπρωτεύουσα** (the co-capital) and is proud of not being Athens. Between the two runs a cheerful, mostly good-natured rivalry, with its own jokes, food arguments, football hatreds and a handful of grammatical shibboleths.

Greeks joke that the country splits at **Λαμία**: *από τη Λαμία και πάνω* (from Lamia up) people say *σε λέω* and eat their μπουγάτσα with the question *κρέμα ή τυρί;*; *από τη Λαμία και κάτω* people say *σου λέω* and order *καλαμάκια*. Like all such jokes it is a caricature, but it tracks a real linguistic boundary: the old dialect split between **northern** and **southern** Greek, first described by the linguist Γεώργιος Χατζιδάκις on the basis of vowels.

Directional verbs follow the map, too. A Thessalonian **κατεβαίνει Αθήνα** (goes *down* to Athens) and an Athenian **ανεβαίνει Θεσσαλονίκη** (goes *up*). Northerners call Athenians, half in jest, **χαμουτζήδες** (the 'down-there people', from *χάμω*, down); Athenians tease northerners about their pronouns, their *παχύ λ* and their sweet frappés.

This lesson gives you what you need to **recognise** northern speech and northern vocabulary, to avoid ordering the wrong thing in either city, and to follow the banter (including sports-fan nicknames, some of which are genuinely offensive). As a learner you should keep **standard (southern) grammar** in your own speech and writing; using northern forms deliberately is a performance, and it only works once you sound fluent.

blocks.title: Η βόρεια αιτιατική: σε λέω, με είπε, σε δίνω
blocks.text:
In standard Greek, the indirect object ('to me', 'to you') of verbs like *λέω, δίνω, στέλνω, φέρνω, δείχνω* is expressed with the **genitive** weak pronoun: *σου λέω* (I tell you), *μου είπε* (he told me), *της έδωσα* (I gave her). Ancient Greek used the dative for this; when the dative died out, the south replaced it with the genitive, and the **north replaced it with the accusative**. So in Macedonia, Thrace, Thessaly, Epirus and Thessaloniki itself you hear:

**Σε λέω**, δεν έρχομαι. *I'm telling you, I'm not coming.*
**Με είπε** να περιμένω. *He told me to wait.*
**Την έδωσα** το κλειδί. *I gave her the key.*
**Δώσε με** ένα τσιγάρο. *Give me a cigarette.*

Linguistically this is not a mistake but a regional variant with a history as long as the southern one; dialectologists list it among the defining features of the northern varieties (in strongly rural northern speech you also get raised vowels: *σι λέου* for *σε λέω*). Socially, though, it is **marked**: schoolteachers correct it, Athenian comedians use it as the quickest way to signal 'northerner', and in formal writing or an exam it counts as an error. Many Thessalonians, conversely, keep it consciously as a badge of identity and lay it on thicker when they are in Athens.

A widely shared internet text claiming that a famous linguist had declared the northern accusative 'more correct' because it is 'closer to the dative' is a fake; the sober view is simply that both systems are legitimate outcomes of the loss of the dative, and the genitive is the standard.

blocks.title: How the northern accusative works (and when it does not apply)
items: It replaces only the **genitive of the indirect object**: μου→με, σου→σε, του→τον, της→την. Plural *μας, σας, τους* look the same in both cases, so you cannot hear the difference there.
It does **not** affect possession: everyone, north and south, says *το σπίτι μου*, never *το σπίτι με*.

It does not touch verbs that take a direct object anyway. *Με είδε* (he saw me), *με πήρε τηλέφωνο* (he called me), *με είπε ψεύτη* (he called me a liar) are **standard** everywhere, because here *με* is the direct object.
So *με είπε* is northern only when it means 'he told me (something)': *με είπε ότι θα αργήσει* (north) = *μου είπε ότι θα αργήσει* (standard).

In more rural northern speech the same switch can affect full noun phrases too (an accusative where the standard has *σε* + accusative or a genitive), but in urban Thessaloniki it is overwhelmingly a matter of the weak pronouns.
Teachers, editors and examiners treat it as an error in writing. Keep *σου λέω* in your own Greek; learn *σε λέω* to understand it, and use it only as a quotation or a joke among friends.

blocks.title: Pronunciation notes
items: *Σε λέω* is pronounced as one stress group, [se ˈleo], often with the *ε* of *λέω* half-swallowed: [se ˈlo]. The emphasis falls on *λέω*; the pronoun is never stressed.
*Πλάκα με κάνεις!* is said with a rising-falling exclamation on *πλά-*; *τι με λες;* is a quick, high-pitched reaction with the stress on *λες*.
*Ξες* is a single syllable [ks̠es], often tacked on at the end of a phrase: *ήταν κλειστό, ξες;* (it was closed, you know?).
The *παχύ λ*: let the back of the tongue rise as for English *full*. Do not try to imitate it on purpose with Thessalonians; an accent caricature is not a compliment.
*Ντεμέκ* is stressed on the last syllable, [deˈmek]; the initial *ντ* is a plain [d] in normal speech.
*Χαμουτζής* [xamuˈdzis]: the *τζ* is the affricate [dz], stress on the end; plural *χαμουτζήδες*.
Mind the stress in *συμπρωτεύουσα* [simbroˈtevusa]: the *μπ* after *συ-* is pronounced [mb].

blocks.title: Fan language: what you will hear at a match
blocks.text:
Greek football (and basketball) culture is tribal, and the language of the **κερκίδα** (stands) is its own register. Organised fan groups take their names from the stadium gates: you will hear *η Θύρα 7* (Olympiakos), *η Θύρα 13* (Panathinaikos), *η Θύρα 4* (PAOK), *η Original 21* (AEK). Basic vocabulary: **ο οπαδός** (fan, supporter; more partisan than *φίλαθλος*), **ο φανατικός**, **το ντέρμπι** (a big derby), **ο διαιτητής** (referee; the universal scapegoat), **το σφύριγμα** (the whistle, a decision), **το πέναλτι**, **το ματς**, **σας πήραμε τα σώβρακα** (we thrashed you, lit. 'we took your underpants').

**Chants** (*συνθήματα*) are a register of their own: rhythmic, often rhyming, frequently obscene (the *γαμώ* family and *πουτάνα* are routine), and sometimes racist or homophobic. Understand them; never repeat them in ordinary company. The cheerful end is self-praise of the *Θρύλε, είσαι η ζωή μου* type; the nasty end targets the rival's origins (*βούλγαροι*, *χανούμισσες*, *γαύροι*), mothers and sexuality. Violence around matches is a serious social problem in Greece, and away fans are often banned altogether, so *η κερκίδα* talk is not just folklore.

In everyday life the football tribe is a quick social marker: *Τι ομάδα είσαι;* (what team are you?) is a standard getting-to-know-you question, and the answer *ΠΑΟΚ* or *Ολυμπιακός* is often taken to say something about where your family comes from. A safe, friendly answer if you have no team: *Δεν έχω ομάδα, υποστηρίζω το καλό ποδόσφαιρο* (I support good football) – expect to be teased for it.

blocks.title: Διάλογος 1: Σουβλάκια με παρεξηγήσεις (Athens, a Thessalonian visits)

items.el: Μαρία: Πεινάς; Πάμε να πάρουμε σουβλάκια από τη γωνία;
items.en: Maria: Hungry? Shall we get souvlaki from the place on the corner?

items.el: Νίκος: Πάμε. Εγώ θέλω μια πίτα γύρο χοιρινό με απ' όλα.
items.en: Nikos: Let's go. I want a pork gyros pita with everything.

items.el: Μαρία: Τυλιχτό γύρο, εννοείς. Κι εγώ δύο καλαμάκια κοτόπουλο.
items.en: Maria: A gyros wrap, you mean. And two chicken skewers for me.

items.el: Νίκος: Καλαμάκια; Τι θα τα κάνεις, θα πιεις φραπέ;
items.en: Nikos: Straws? What for, are you having a frappé?

items.el: Μαρία: Χαχα, όχι ρε! Καλαμάκια, σουβλάκια στο ξυλάκι!
items.en: Maria: Haha, no! Kalamakia, meat on a stick!

items.el: Νίκος: Α, σουβλάκια, πες το έτσι. Σε μας καλαμάκι είναι αυτό που ρουφάς τον καφέ.
items.en: Nikos: Oh, souvlakia, say so. Back home a kalamaki is what you suck your coffee through.

items.el: Μαρία: Εντάξει. Να πάρουμε και μια λεμονάδα;
items.en: Maria: OK. Shall we get a lemonade too?

items.el: Νίκος: Ναι αφού. Αλλά κανονική, ε; Με λεμόνι.
items.en: Nikos: Sure. But a proper one, right? With lemons.

items.el: Μαρία: Εδώ λεμονάδα είναι το αναψυκτικό με τις φούσκες, φίλε.
items.en: Maria: Here lemonade is the fizzy soft drink, mate.

items.el: Νίκος: Πλάκα με κάνεις. Και αύριο το πρωί μπουγάτσα;
items.en: Nikos: You're kidding me. And bougatsa tomorrow morning?

items.el: Μαρία: Ναι, θα πάρω μία με κρέμα.
items.en: Maria: Yes, I'll get one with cream.

items.el: Νίκος: Δεν θα σε ρωτήσει ο φούρναρης «κρέμα ή τυρί»;
items.en: Nikos: Won't the baker ask you 'cream or cheese?'

items.el: Μαρία: Εδώ μπουγάτσα σκέτο σημαίνει κρέμα. Χαμουτζήδες είμαστε, τι να κάνουμε.
items.en: Maria: Here plain 'bougatsa' means cream. We're southerners, what can you do.

items.el: Νίκος: Εσύ το είπες, όχι εγώ!
items.en: Nikos: You said it, not me!

blocks.text:
**Common mistakes and false friends**

• **καλαμάκι** is a skewer in Athens and a **straw** in Thessaloniki. Ordering *δύο καλαμάκια* in a Thessaloniki grill gets you a puzzled look; asking for *ένα καλαμάκι* with your frappé in Athens is fine.
• **τυρί** in Thessaloniki means **feta**; if you want yellow cheese, say *κασέρι*.
• **λεμονάδα** in an Athenian souvlaki place is usually a fizzy soft drink.
• **αλοιφή** is a creamy salad or dip in Thessaloniki, but **ointment** everywhere else: *βάλε αλοιφή* in Athens sounds like a pharmacy.
• Don't 'learn' *σε λέω, με είπε* as an alternative you may use in writing: it will be marked wrong. But don't 'correct' a Thessalonian either.
• *Με είπε βλάκα* (he called me an idiot) is **not** northern: *λέω κάποιον κάτι* = to call someone something takes the accusative everywhere.
• **Πάνε** in Thessaloniki is the imperative 'go!'; in Athens it is usually 'they go'.
• **βούλγαρος** as a name for northerners or PAOK fans is a slur (4/5), not banter. **χαμουτζής** is light banter (1-2).
• Don't imitate the *παχύ λ* or *σι λέου* to someone's face; accent caricature is the Athenian side of the rivalry at its worst.

blocks.title: Θεσσαλονίκη: a city of layers, and why its Greek sounds the way it does
blocks.text:
Thessaloniki was an Ottoman city from 1430 to 1912, and for most of that time its largest community was **Sephardic Jewish**: Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 settled there in great numbers, and Ladino (Judeo-Spanish) was the city's street language; it was called *la madre de Israel*. Turkish, Greek, Ladino, Bulgarian, Albanian and French were all heard in its markets. The great fire of 1917, the Greco-Turkish **population exchange** of 1923, and above all the **deportation of the Jewish community to Auschwitz in 1943**, in which the overwhelming majority was murdered, transformed it into an almost wholly Greek-speaking city.

The population exchange also brought tens of thousands of **refugees** from Asia Minor, Eastern Thrace, Constantinople and the Black Sea (**Pontus**), and Macedonia remains the heartland of Pontic Greek culture today (see next lesson). Two of Greece's great football clubs carry this history in their names: **ΠΑΟΚ** stands for *Πανθεσσαλονίκειος Αθλητικός Όμιλος Κωνσταντινουπολιτών*, and Athens' **ΑΕΚ** for *Αθλητική Ένωση Κωνσταντινουπόλεως*; both took the Byzantine **double-headed eagle** as their emblem.

You can taste the layers. **Μπουγάτσα** goes back, via Medieval Greek *πογάτσα*, to Late Latin *focacia*; **τσουρέκι** is from Turkish *çörek*; **ντεμέκ** is from Turkish *demek* ('that is to say'), and in Thessaloniki it narrowed to 'supposedly'. The city's 'Πολίτικη' (Constantinopolitan) cooking, its syrup-soaked **τρίγωνα Πανοράματος**, its tsipouro joints, and its **φραπές** (improvised at the Thessaloniki International Fair, **ΔΕΘ**, in 1957 when a Nescafé representative shook instant coffee with cold water) all feed Thessalonian pride.

Athens in turn is mocked from the north as noisy, arrogant and self-absorbed (*αθηνοκεντρισμός*), while Athenians patronise Thessaloniki as *επαρχία* with a seafront. Both cities secretly envy the other: Athenians envy Thessaloniki's food, its walkable seafront, its student life and its film festival; Thessalonians envy Athens' sunshine, concerts, theatres and sheer size. The rivalry is affectionate enough that a slang lexicon calls it, mockingly, **ο καβγάς της μπουγάτσας**: a quarrel over pastry.

blocks.title: Σαλονικιός στην Αθήνα
blocks.text:
Σαλονικιός στην Αθήνα: τα πρώτα μου σοκ (μακρύ, σόρι)

Παιδιά, έξι μήνες τώρα μένω Αθήνα για δουλειά και λέω να σας τα πω, γιατί αν δεν τα πω κάπου θα σκάσω.

Πρώτη μέρα, μπαίνω σε ένα σουβλατζίδικο στο Παγκράτι και λέω «δύο καλαμάκια και μια λεμονάδα». Ο τύπος μου φέρνει δύο σουβλάκια χοιρινά και ένα αναψυκτικό με ανθρακικό. Εγώ ήθελα καλαμάκι για τον φραπέ μου, ρε! Και λεμονάδα κανονική, με λεμόνι. «Πλάκα με κάνεις», του λέω. Με κοίταξε σαν εξωγήινο.

Δεύτερο σοκ: ζητάω μια πίτα γύρο και ο άλλος με ρωτάει «τυλιχτό θες;». Τυλιχτό, ξες, λες και μιλάμε για χαλί.

Τρίτο: στον φούρνο ζητάω μπουγάτσα. Περιμένω την ερώτηση «κρέμα ή τυρί;». Τίποτα. Μου δίνει κρέμα, ντεμέκ αυτονόητο. Και όταν ζήτησα τυρί για τη σαλάτα, μου έδωσε κασέρι! Τυρί είναι η φέτα, ρε παιδιά, τι να λέμε τώρα.

Στη δουλειά, την πρώτη εβδομάδα, λέω στη συνάδελφο «σε είπα να με στείλεις το αρχείο». Γέλασε τόσο που κόντεψε να πέσει από την καρέκλα. Από τότε με φωνάζει «Θεσσαλονίκη» και κάθε φορά που μιλάω μιμείται το παχύ μου λ. Εντάξει, δεν παρεξηγιέμαι, έχει πλάκα. Αλλά να ξέρετε ότι κι εμείς σας λέμε χαμουτζήδες, οπότε πάτσι.

Το αστικό εδώ το λένε λεωφορείο. Κι όταν έπαθα φούιτ με το ποδήλατο, ο μάστορας δεν καταλάβαινε τι του έλεγα. «Λάστιχο, φίλε, σ' έπιασε λάστιχο», με διόρθωσε.

Τα καλά τώρα: η Αθήνα έχει τα πάντα. Συναυλίες κάθε βράδυ, θέατρα, βόλτες στα Εξάρχεια με τους κουλτουριάρηδες φίλους μου. Ήπια και έναν καφέ στο Κολωνάκι, μία φορά. Τον πλήρωσα όσο ένα τραπέζι τσίπουρα στη Σαλονίκη. Δεν ξαναπάω.

Ποδόσφαιρο δεν συζητάω στη δουλειά. Μισοί είναι βάζελοι, μισοί γαύροι, και όταν έμαθαν ότι είμαι ΠΑΟΚ, ένας με είπε «Βούλγαρο» για πλάκα. Του εξήγησα ήρεμα ότι αυτή η πλάκα είναι βαριά, το κατάλαβε και ζήτησε συγγνώμη. Από τότε με λέει «Δικέφαλε» και είμαστε μια χαρά.

Μου λείπει η παραλία, μου λείπει να λέω «τα λέμε στην Καμάρα», μου λείπει η Τούμπα. Αλλά, να πω την αλήθεια, έχω αρχίσει να λέω κι εγώ «μου λες». Μη με κράξετε. Πάνε, γράψτε κι εσείς τα δικά σας σοκ από κάτω!
blocks.en:
A Thessalonian in Athens: my first culture shocks (long, sorry)

Folks, I've been living in Athens for six months for work and I thought I'd tell you, because if I don't tell someone I'll burst.

First day, I walk into a souvlaki place in Pangrati and say 'two kalamakia and a lemonade'. The guy brings me two pork skewers and a fizzy soft drink. I wanted a straw for my frappé, man! And proper lemonade, with lemons. 'You're kidding me,' I tell him. He looked at me like an alien.

Second shock: I ask for a gyros pita and the other guy asks me 'you want a wrap (tylichto)?'. Tylichto, you know, as if we were talking about a carpet.

Third: at the bakery I ask for bougatsa. I wait for the question 'cream or cheese?'. Nothing. She gives me cream, supposedly the obvious choice. And when I asked for cheese for the salad, she gave me kasseri! Cheese means feta, guys, what can I say.

At work, in the first week, I say to a colleague 'se ipa na me stileis to arheio' (northern for 'I told you to send me the file'). She laughed so hard she almost fell off her chair. Since then she calls me 'Thessaloniki' and every time I speak she imitates my thick l. Fine, I don't take offence, it's funny. But you should know that we call you hamoutzides, so we're even.

The astiko (city bus) is called leoforeio here. And when I got a fouit (flat tyre) on my bike, the mechanic didn't understand what I was telling him. 'A flat, mate, you've got a flat (s' epiase lasticho)', he corrected me.

Now the good things: Athens has everything. Concerts every night, theatres, walks in Exarchia with my culture-snob friends. I also had a coffee in Kolonaki, once. I paid as much as a whole table of tsipouro in Thessaloniki. Never again.

I don't discuss football at work. Half are Panathinaikos fans, half Olympiakos fans, and when they found out I'm PAOK, one guy called me 'Bulgarian' as a joke. I calmly explained that this joke is heavy, he got it and apologised. Since then he calls me 'Double-Headed Eagle' and we get on fine.

I miss the seafront, I miss saying 'see you at the Kamara', I miss Toumba. But, to tell the truth, I've started saying 'mou les' myself. Don't trash me for it. Go on, write your own shocks below!

gloss.Πλάκα με κάνεις: πλάκα με κάνεις — you're kidding me (northern: με for μου)
gloss.πίτα γύρο: πίτα γύρο — gyros in pita (northern way of ordering)
gloss.τυλιχτό: τυλιχτό — Athenian word for the pita wrap
gloss.μπουγάτσα: μπουγάτσα — filo pie; Thessaloniki asks: cream or cheese?
gloss.κρέμα ή τυρί: κρέμα ή τυρί; — cream or cheese? (bougatsa question)
gloss.κασέρι: κασέρι — yellow cheese (in Thessaloniki: any yellow cheese)
gloss.Τυρί: τυρί — in Thessaloniki: feta by default
gloss.σε είπα να με στείλεις: σε είπα / με στείλεις — northern for σου είπα / μου στείλεις
gloss.παχύ μου λ: παχύ λ — the velarised 'dark' l of Macedonia
gloss.σ' έπιασε λάστιχο: μ' έπιασε λάστιχο — I've got a flat (Athens)
gloss.Εξάρχεια: Εξάρχεια — Athens district: students, anarchists, bars
gloss.τσίπουρα: τσίπουρο — grape spirit; πάμε για τσίπουρα = go out for tsipouro and meze
gloss.ΠΑΟΚ: ΠΑΟΚ — Thessaloniki club founded by Constantinopolitan refugees
gloss.Βούλγαρο: βούλγαρος — slur for PAOK fans / northerners (4/5)
gloss.Δικέφαλε: Δικέφαλος — double-headed eagle; nickname of PAOK (and AEK)
gloss.Καμάρα: Καμάρα — Arch of Galerius, classic meeting point
